Our best Dining experience in Siagon
Sep 2026 • Couples
The food was fantastic, the restaurant was packed, we were walk ins and the staff could not help enough. The front of house staff assisted us with our selections and the shared appetiser platter was really fantastic. 

They then assisted with ordering mains which included a divine prawn and squid dish served with tea leaves which were a highlight of the dish.

Then a sea bass with pineapple which was beautifully presented and very tasty.
 
We had some traditional Vietnamese deserts which included mung beans which we would never order however recommended by the staff. They were very different to us however the flavours and textures were really beautiful and would definitely order again.

The service was very attentive and prompt. The table next to us was on the third sitting as we were leaving.

The kitchen obviously highly talented and very well organised as food service was prompt. 

The location was walking distance from hotel on the river and will be close to everywhere and transport is really good value on the Grab although we did walk most places. 

This was fourth dinner we had in Siagon and whilst it cost a little more it was really good value for money and this restaurant was easily the best of the four on every measurement.

Not to the owners Google our online maps took us to the incorrect place as the restaurant is situated back off the street in a well lite walkway. It has obviously happened before as the security at the hotel where we were directed advised us to head down the road and turn right and right so it has happened before.

We are so happy we found the Hoa Tuc in Siagon and will definitely go next time as there were easily 7 or 8 things on the menu that we would be happy to have.

Insider tip:
We were walk ins and lucky to get a table. Worth while making a booking. Google maps takes you to the wrong place even with correct address.

My First Michelin-Recommended Vietnamese Restaurant
May 2026 • Family
I was curious about the quality, and the restaurant looked beautiful with its classic vibe, so I decided to give it a try. 

Overall, the food was good. The ingredients were fresh, and everything was cooked really well. The meat was tender, the vegetables were fresh, and every dish felt light and enjoyable. As a Vietnamese, though, I found the flavors a bit too mild. They're balanced and easy to eat, but I personally prefer something a little more flavorful. I think the seasoning would suit foreigners who are trying Vietnamese food for the first time. The price is quite high compared to a regular Vietnamese meal, but the service was great and the whole experience was worth it. I'd recommend trying it at least once.

The Food:
 • Starters:
 • Cá thác lác chiên giòn (Crispy featherback fish cakes): Perfectly cooked and full of flavor.
 • Bò lá lốt (Grilled minced beef wrapped in betel leaf): A standout dish, tender and packed with aromatic spices.
 • Mains:
 • Sườn non mật ong nướng (Grilled honey pork ribs): Sweet, savory, and perfectly tender, complemented by pickled shallots and lemongrass.
 • Cà tím xào sốt sa tế / Cà tím nướng (Eggplant with saté sauce / Grilled eggplant): Both variations were delicious, but the saté sauce added a delightful kick.

The Service:
The staff were friendly, attentive, and genuinely welcoming, which enhanced our overall dining experience.

Hoa Túc is a must-visit for anyone looking to explore the vibrant flavors of Vietnamese cuisine in a unique and historic setting. We can’t wait to return!

The restaurant I love
Jun 2023 • Friends
Hoa Tuc - one of the Vietnamese restaurants that perhaps everyone who works in the tourism industry in Saigon and foreigners living here has heard of at least once. Personally, in Saigon - where the F&B market is very competitive and new restaurants spring up and close frequently, Hoa Tuc is truly a highlight. I've always wanted to have restaurants that I could go to this year and come back next year and still find the old feeling. I've been to Hoa Tuc 5 times, both for lunch and dinner, and both times I saw a lot of customers. At noon, the weather in Saigon is hot, so customers are usually given tables to sit indoors, the ground floor will be for individual customers while tour guests are taken to the 2nd floor to sit separately so that the restaurant can serve more easily, depending on the situation. But in the evening, the outside seating space is the most ideal because Saigon is hot during the day and cools down very quickly in the evening. The atmosphere around this alley is also very pleasant with the sound of music and jingling cutlery. You will feel like you are sitting somewhere other than in Vietnam when you see mostly foreigners around you. The dishes of Hoa Tuc's set menu are Vietnamese but prepared in European culinary style, quite harmonious in terms of food combination and quantity. Usually the restaurant will serve 1 dish per dish for 2 guests and guests can take their own meals so it is relatively easy. Hoa Tuc's food decoration is not fussy but still requires investment, not simply on a plate/bowl like a pure Vietnamese restaurant. The staff wears uniforms, with the Hoa Tuc logo embroidered on their shirts, very neat and cute. Fast and enthusiastic service attitude, good English communication ability with guests.

For our last night in Vietnam we decided to go somewhere with a nicer atmosphere but we still wanted Vietnamese food (because we haven’t had enough of them). So after researching on TA and reading very good reviews about Hoa Tuc, we happily arrived at the restaurant. The place had a great atmosphere and we were the last guests that didn’t have to wait for a table. We usually would open a bottle of wine in such occasion but we were thirsty and ordered two beers first. The menu looked really good and the prices were fair (considering its ambience, location, English speaking staff, etc). We ordered four dishes, being a fried tofu with lemongrass, tofu and sweet potato curry, braised pork and egg in claypot, and caramelized prawns in claypot. The fried tofu with lemongrass was served first, and we were stunned. The tofu were pan seared, tough and dense and lukewarm at the most at the center, making the soybean taste very distinctive. It was topped with dried shredded pork and chopped lemongrass, and the entire thing was tasteless. We immediately asked for the Vietnamese chilli sauce try to save the dish, where the server brought us soy sauce with sliced red chilli explaining she forgot to bring us this dipping sauce for the dish. In essence, it was tofu dipping in soy sauce. We comforted ourselves maybe we ordered an off item from the menu, and remained positive on the other dishes. Followed were the curry and the braised pork, the curry’s taste was average at most, it seems they tried to give a lot of a ingredient in this vegetarian dish so diners feel “bang for their bucks”, but the balance between how much vegetables and curry in the dish was off. The braised pork and egg tasted similar to a dish called “Lu Rou Fan” from a Taiwan, however the pork was very tough where it suppose to be fork tender. The sauce of the finale caramelized prawns tasted ok (would be salty if you had a lighter taste), but the butterflied prawns were overcooked, what a waste. We finished our beer before the prawns were served, and being pretty heavy drinkers ourselves, we were so discouraged with the food and just did not want to order another drink (contemplated on sharing a bottle of beer to wash down the food as no water were served, but we decided we didn’t want to prolong our dinner). Being a foodie myself, I have spent over half of my life in Asia and have 30+ years in tasting Asian food, although I’m no expert in Vietnamese food, the food we had were definitely subpar to all other Vietnamese food we have had before, and definitely was poorly prepared Asian food. So if you are reading this review, please be more adventurous and try the street food and local small shops, although they are unsanitary, but they give you a real taste of good food.

I went to Hoa Tuc with a group of colleagues while on a business trip. The food we had was very enjoyable and while not everything went perfectly, the service was friendly and responsive.
The restaurant is centrally located in the city, within easy walking distance of many large international hotels. It is located in the area of a former opium refinery, in an alley that has a number of other restaurants. A local pointed to this area as a good "first stop" to find food in this part of Saigon as there is a variety of restaurants there and they are all good. Hoa Tuc has both indoor and outdoor seating and we opted for being outdoors. We got a nice table, a bit behind the building, not out of the way but not in any walkway either. The decor of the restaurant is very nice, especially for those appreciating Art Nouveau style.
The menu is primarily Vietnamese, but it has a wide range of types of dishes, so most everyone should fine something they like. We opted to share a plate of appetizers and then each selected a main dish. I opted for lemongrass bbq beef with rice noodles, vegetables and rice paper for rolling. The appetizers were good and the main dish was very good. The meat was flavorful, the vegetables fresh, the herbs were excellent and the dipping sauce was classic. My colleagues were overall very satisfied as well, with the exception of two who had stir fried beef that turned out chewy and had their dishes then replaced by a new selection.
The service was very good; helpful and friendly, and most of the time it was prompt, but the restaurant was quite busy so sometimes there was a short wait. We were a group of about eight people so finding a table was not trivial, but that was solved quickly. Throughout the dinner, service was good overall and willing to provide what we requested. As for my colleagues who were unhappy with their beef, they quickly received the option of choosing another dish. So, not perfect, but great willingness to make things right.
I would happily eat at Hoa Tuc again when in Saigon.

I have been dining at Hoa Tuc for the past 4 years. While I am not a regular, I happen to go in many occasions, for business or leisure, throughout the year. I must say, I was never disappointed. 

What I like is that I can bring visitors (usually friends from Europe, US or Australia) to this restaurant and be sure that they will not be disappointed either. The menu has not changed over the past 4 years... and it is not a sin. They put together a very sensible selection of great food mostly based on Vietnamese recipes... but just "mostly"... actually the cooking style in many cases is kind of westernized and this is why first time visitors can be introduced to Vietnamese food through a safe stop to Hoa Tuc before trying hard core real Vietnamese food in other venues. 

You can order their Vietnamese rolls as appetizer, they will show you how to roll them... (it is food, no pun intended). I personally like their seafood (snapper and seabass) and I never forget to order their excellent soft shell crabs. 

The place can be quite crowded and sometimes service is not impeccable, but I am usually happy about the overall experience. The place is in an alley (I should say an enclave) where there used to be an opium refinery. It now hosts a half dozen restaurants. Hoa Tuc is just one of them.

I should also mention that they run a popular Vietnamese cuisine crash course that can be a nice idea for spending a few hours.

Contemporary Vietnamese
Jun 2014 • Friends
Hoa Tuc is a modern, sophisticated Vietnamese restaurant located in an alley that also contains several other well-regarded additions to the international dining possibilities in Ho Chi Minh City. We went for lunch on a hot summer afternoon. The interior’s floral decoration and air conditioning were welcome relief. We shared three dishes that arrived in sequence with sufficient time to enjoy each one and lingered to enjoy a final Vietnamese iced coffee. 
The first dish was a banana flower salad that was a perfectly refreshing combination of the shredded flower and chicken with traditional elements of fish sauce, lime, peanuts, fried shallots, and fresh herbs. The second dish was a wonderful variation on the classic summer roll with shrimp in rice paper wrappers. In addition to the useful internal ingredients, this one had a leaf of spicy mustard greens adhering to the outside of the wrapper. The final dish was a delicate barbequed spare ribs accented with five spice powder. 
The restaurant has an extensive wine list that is moderately priced by western standards. For those drinking alcohol, beer is more usual, but the crisp white wine that was the restaurant’s selection of the month was an excellent accompaniment, proving that a judicious wine choice can turn a classic Vietnamese meal into a true feast for all aspects of the palate. 
Prices are on the European scale, which is becoming increasingly common for this type of restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City. But given the high quality, we did not feel that the cost was excessive – just more than what most Vietnamese would think of paying for a meal at a restaurant.

Between us we ordered Hoa Tuc salad; BBQ sea bass with mango avocado salsa served with small rounds of sweet potato and taro; and seared beef salad. Also tried two glasses of the house wine. The two salads were really tasty, combining Vietnamese flavors in the dressings with local veggies, prawns and beef. Very beautiful, too. The sea bass, on the other hand, had some nice flavors, but the salsa featured mostly tomatoes (I did see a fleck of green and orange in there, but not much), so didn't have that complex combination of flavors that I was hoping for. It was also barely warm. It was served with 3 small sliced/rounds of sweet potato lined next to three small rounds of taro. They were definitely not hot, and were pretty tasteless. The presentation was a bit weird. 
The place, as I said, was packed and even with that , the service was good. 
As far as the wine goes, ordering wine by the glass in a tropical place is probably in general a bad idea. I keep hoping there will be an exception to the rule, but I haven't found it yet. We were in a rush when the waiter came not wanting him to get away, and resorted to trying a glass of the house red. Got pretty much what we expected. Our bad. 
All in all, if you want a nice spot to sit in the evening, this could be it. In District 1, within walking distance of most of the big hotels downtown, it's located in an 'alley' that actually used to be the location of the opium factory in Saigon. In fact Hoa Tuc means opium flower. There are a few other restaurants in this same small area, but it's relatively quiet and is very pleasant. Probably coming earlier in the evening, you could avoid some of the crowd. Having reservations is a very good idea, especially if you're coming with more than two people. We'll definitely go back. If you're just looking for great Vietnamese food, try one of those spots on almost any street where you see lots of local people eating.

Great place, good food, but the wine?
Sep 2011
The setting in a courtyard with comfortable seating was excellent. So was the food and service. The cost of food in the 15-25 usd was good value for a special night or just those wanting a higher standard.
I don't think this was matched by the wine despite the claim on their site.
Most wines were about 600,000vnd. The most expensive at 1,500,000 vnd or 75USD was Wither Hills sauvignon blanc. I am very familiar with this wine, over many vintages, and it is good to very good quality wine with the flavours likely to match the freshness of the food.
It retails in NZ at around 13.50 us, and in a restaurant might go for 31-forty five although there would be resistance at that level, as you can often buy it at 11 the probable wholesale price including tax.
On investigation I found the total tax on wine is 80% tariff plus 17.5% on the total ie 100%. There is the culprit. I found the retail price of the probable importer and calculate that the probable markup on wholesale is close to 200% which is fair and not excessive.
The problem is likely that there is a buyer resistance when ordinary reasonable wine say exceeds the cost of two mains. Not talking the rich just reasonably wine knowledgeable people who can generally roughly gauge a wine as pretty good or not.
Now if the top wine on the list had a 13.50 usd retail what about the bulk of the list which if my memory is correct was in the 500,000 1,000,000 range a 1/3 -2/3?
Well obviously I am not familiar with the names of most of these. Two whites were available by the glass. One a chardonnay from Spain at around 5-6 usd I had to try from disbelief anyone would offer such a thing. It had only two things going for it - it was clear and alcoholic. The second was a reisling at about 7.50. It had some flavour though at that price I could resist a second glass.
This isn't a criticism of the restaurant, although I have some scepticism about their claims on wine on their website rather the tax is the problem, along with an attempt to limit the wine prices to offset this.
Just bear it in mind. A cheap sparkling or even beer may be better.

My favourite during our HCMC visit.
Hoa Tuc is located in a court yard shared by The Refinery, Vasco's and others. Look for the archway across the road from the Park Hyatt. 
We ate here several times because we found the menu was extensive and included a daily fresh seafood specials menu. Dishes like cockles, razor clams, etc, give you an insight into the variety of Vietnamese cuisine. 
If you only had one day in town I would suggest this place because you can try multiple tasting platters of starters, mains and desserts to share with your group. You can even try the famous local Banh Xeo here, and be shown how to eat it like the locals. 
They will show you the wrap and roll technique here which you will understand once you have visited Vietnam. The staff are great and are proud to tell you about the food that Vietnam offers. 
There are inside and outside dining options, they also run a cooking class I believe, but we just ran out of time. If you are a "foodie" and have a list of items to try whilst in Vietnam, this is a pretty good place to start. I just wanted to go back until I had tried everything on the menu. 
And yes, if you walk inside to the bar.......you will see it.......that big jar.....with a huge cobra inside suspended in a bath of herbs and rice alcohol. I had to try it. Funny enough it tasted better than I thought because of the herbs, sort of like Jagermeister on steroids. If you want to try it they ask "Are you sure?" and if you go ahead they use a ladle to carefully fill a large shot glass, and then also hand you a big glass of ice water.
When you ask "Why do Vietnamese drink this?" The answer is, with a smile, "Because it is good for the man!" I should have known.
